note:
The opening words indicate both the historical starting point of the book and the theological crisis with which it deals. Moses’s death, recorded at the end of Deuteronomy, concludes the judgment of God on the generation that came out of Egypt (5:4–6; Deut. 1:35; 32:51). What is to be said now that Moses has died and the people of Israel have fallen under God’s judgment? Ch. 1 introduces the answer to this question, namely, that even “after the death of Moses” the Lord is faithful to His promises. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes. This reality and its consequences are spelled out by God to Joshua (vv. 1–9), and then by Joshua to the people in general (vv. 10, 11) and the two-and-a-half tribes in particular (vv. 12–15). Finally, the people’s response is recorded (vv. 16–18).

**1:1 the servant of the** LORD **.** This title of honor, first given to Moses in Deut. 34:5, recalls the special role of Moses in God’s purposes (vv. 1, 2, 7, 13, 15; cf. Is. 42:1). It is later applied to Joshua at his death (24:29).

**Joshua.** Joshua’s name was changed from Hoshea (“salvation”) to Joshua (“the Lord is salvation”) by Moses (Num. 13:16). Joshua appears as Moses’s assistant as early as Ex. 17. He was one of the men sent from Kadesh-barnea to explore the land (Num. 13:8), and he joined Caleb in calling on the Israelites to trust the Lord and not to rebel against Him (Num. 14:6–9). Like Caleb (Deut. 1:36), he escaped the judgment that fell on that generation because of its refusal to obey God at Kadesh-barnea. Joshua is here presented as the successor to Moses, as was anticipated before Moses’s death (Num. 27:12–23; Deut. 3:28; 31:1–8). Joshua’s role, however, continues to be subordinate to that of Moses. This is expressed in his submission to the “Book of the Law” (1:8 note) and his obedience to the commands of Moses, something repeatedly emphasized throughout the book (e.g., 1:7; 8:31; 11:12, 15; 14:2, 5; 20:2).

Importantly, Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim and as a descendant of Joseph may well have been viewed by his contemporaries as belonging to the unique family line through which God would establish a monarchy in Israel. Only later, in the time of Samuel, would the tribe of Ephraim be rejected by God in favor of the tribe of Judah (cf. Ps. 78:67–72), though this development is anticipated as early as Joseph’s lifetime (Gen. 49:8–10).

The people are east of the river (Deut. 1:1), which forms a boundary between them and the land God promised to the west. See also 3:15.

**into the land.** The land is God’s gift to the Israelites, in faithfulness to His promise to Abraham (see vv. 3, 6). This is the dominant theme of the book: note the elaboration of this idea in 24:13, echoing Deut. 6:10, 11. See note on 21:43.
“Your” and “you” are plural, indicating the promise is addressed to all Israel.

The extent of the land promised here exceeds what is actually received in the days of Joshua and corresponds to the dimensions of Solomon’s kingdom (1 Kin. 4:21). Despite the emphasis on fulfillment in Joshua (21:45 note), the book sees the promise as still pointing to the future (13:1 note; 23:5, 12–13).

These promises are addressed to Joshua individually, as the successor to Moses. The section begins and ends with God’s promise to be with him. Near the end is the exhortation to be strong and courageous. In the middle is the commandment to keep God’s instructions, along with the promise of success if he does. In ch. 23 Joshua applies these ideas to the whole people of Israel in the light of the faithfulness of God, which the whole book proclaims.

**1:5 I will be with you.** See Gen. 26:3 and notes; Ex. 3:12. The divine presence is not a general concept or a mystical experience, but rather the presence of God to fulfill His promises. Cf. the promise of Jesus in Matt. 28:20.

Confidence based on the promises of God is the essence of biblical faith (vv. 9, 18; 8:1; 10:8, 25; 11:6).

**inherit.** The land as an inheritance is important in this book. An inheritance is something handed down from the past, as the land was first given in the divine oath made to Abraham (Gen. 15:18–21) and subsequently restated to Isaac and Jacob (Gen 26:3–4; 28:13–15).

The essential relationship between faith and obedience is illustrated here. Faith is confidence based on God’s promise (v. 6), and such faith bears the fruit of obedience (v. 7).

**the law.** The Hebrew word is broader in meaning than the English word “law”; a better translation is “instruction” (see 1:8). See theological note “Special Revelation and the Bible” on p. 142.

**have good success.** Success is understood in terms of what God has promised. Such success cannot be understood simply as a reward earned by obedience, because the promise is issued before any obedience. It is more accurate to understand the promised success as something that can be forfeited by disobedience. Ultimately, however, God preserves an inheritance for His elect (Rom. 8:28–30).

The material recorded by Moses after he spoke to the Israelites in the wilderness east of the Jordan. It probably refers to all that is now preserved in Deut. 5:1–26:19. According to Deut. 17:18–19, Israelite kings must make a copy of the Book of the Law and meditate upon it every day in order to know how to lead the people of Israel. The Israelites will be judged by God on the basis of their obedience to the Book of the Law. Deut. 31:24–26 records how Moses wrote this book and entrusted it to the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant. See 8:34–35; 23:6; 24:26.

**meditate.** Cf. Ps. 1:2. From meditation on the Book of the Law flow all the consequences of the promise already seen in vv. 6, 7: obedience and success (v. 8); faith and the presence of God (v. 9).

While it is also possible that “three days” is not a precise expression and means “a few days,” it seems best to understand it here as a precise length of time.

**to possess.** The promise that God has given (v. 2) demands the human act of taking possession, an act of obedience that demonstrates true faith (vv. 6; 18:3; and notes).

Num. 32 shows how the Reubenites, Gad­ites, and half-tribe of Manasseh (13:8 note) have already received their portion of land east of the Jordan. It has been understood that they will join in Israel’s conquest of the western portion of the Promised Land (Num. 32:16–32; Deut. 3:18–20). All Israel must participate in taking possession of the whole land. There is a dramatic sequel in ch. 22. See notes on 12:1; 13:8–33.

See also v. 15. The goal of God’s gift of the land is often referred to as “rest” (11:23; 21:44; 22:4; 23:1), a condition or state that links the land with God’s purposes in creation (Gen. 2:2, 3). For the NT extension of this idea, see Heb. 3:7–4:11.

The people’s obedient response to Joshua, and therefore to God, will be echoed and elaborated at the end of the book (24:16–24). The essential connection between faith and obedience is implicit: the obedience of the people is not meritorious in any sense for salvation; nevertheless, it provides unambiguous evidence that they believe the Lord’s promise (cf. James 2:14–26 and notes). The necessary qualities for Joshua’s leadership are that God is with him (v. 5 note) and that he is a man of faith (v. 6 note).

The Israelites divide and conquer the land in a series of three campaigns. They start with a central campaign (chs. 2–8), then progress to a southern campaign (chs. 9–10), and finally march on the northern territory (ch. 11). The first major section of the book recounts the movement of the Israelites from Shittim (2:1), across the Jordan River (chs. 3; 4; cf. 1:2), and into the center of the land of Canaan. This movement marks the end of one era (5:9) and the beginning of the new life in the Land of Promise (5:12). It is the book’s first main testimony to God’s faithfulness to His promises.

**2:1–24** Before the expected sequel to ch. 1 (see 3:1), there is the surprising story of the spies who return to Joshua proclaiming the promise of God (v. 24; cf. 1:2–5). Although the book of Joshua describes in graphic detail the defeat of the Canaanites (chs. 6–12), it gives a prominent place to Rahab, a Canaanite harlot (6:17). It is from her lips that the spies hear testimony to the promise and the power of God (vv. 9–11), wherein she seeks and finds His kindness (vv. 12–14). She will be spared from the coming judgment (6:22, 23) and find a place among the people of God (6:25). The chapter testifies to the grace of God in bringing such a woman to seek and find His mercy. The story of Rahab supplies an important perspective on the judgments of God that occupy much of this book.

**2:1 Shittim.** The site is a reminder of a time when Israel was guilty of harlotry (both physical and spiritual; Num. 25:1–3), a time not forgotten in this book (22:17).

**spies.** The role of these spies is as unusual as the conquest to follow. Both their role and the conquest are shaped by the promise of God. See their report in v. 24; cf. Num. 13:17–20.

**prostitute ... Rahab.** The narrative does not say why the spies choose Rahab’s house. She is remembered in the NT as an ancestor of David and of Christ through her marriage to Salmon (Matt. 1:5) and as an example of faith (Heb. 11:31) and good works (James 2:25).
The Israelites invade a Canaan made up of city-states, each with its own king.
The skillfully narrated story creates a moment of tension before telling the reader that the men have been hidden (v. 4).

Undoubtedly Rahab did know (v. 9). The writer of Joshua does not justify or condemn Rahab’s deception, although her actions clearly save the lives of the Israelite spies (vv. 9–11). In the NT, James approves Rahab’s rescue of the spies because it was an act of faith based on the belief that God would give Jericho to the Israelites (James 2:25).
Note the narrative style in which information is given out of chronological sequence. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.
The suspense of the narrative increases, since the spies now seem to be trapped.

Rahab knows what God wants Israel to know (3:10), namely, that the promise of God is true.

**fear.** This is the inevitable response to finding oneself on the wrong side of what God has promised to do (cf. 1:6). God’s destruction of the Egyptian army is a warning to the people of Canaan, though few Canaanites besides Rahab heed it (5:1; 9:24; 10:2; cf. Ex. 15:14–16; Deut. 2:25).

The cause of Rahab’s knowledge, and the Canaanites’ terror, is the news of what God has already done for Israel in faithfulness to His promises. See note on 9:3.

**Amorites.** The term is flexible, sometimes applying to all the peoples of Canaan (e.g., 24:15), sometimes more specifically to people in the hill country (e.g., 5:1), especially as distinct from the Jebusites, who also occupied the hill country (e.g., 3:10).

**Sihon and Og.** See note on 12:2–5.

**destruction.** See notes on 6:17, 18.
LORD **your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.** The acknowledgment of God required in Israel (Deut. 4:39) is made by Rahab.

The Hebrew word often refers to God’s mercy to Israel in accordance with His promises.

**a sure sign.** Probably the oath (v. 14).
The mercy sought presupposes the certainty of the promise of God. It is no less than deliverance from the coming wrath (cf. 1 Thess. 1:10).
LORD **gives us the land.** The certainty of the promise is again assumed.

verse_quote: she let them down ... the city wall.
note: The suspense created in vv. 2, 3, 7 is resolved.

The cord is not mentioned in ch. 6. It is unlikely that symbolic significance should be seen in the color, although allegorical readings have sometimes associated the cord with the blood of the Passover lamb and the blood of Christ.
LORD **has given.** These spies return with the news that the promise of God is indeed certain (1:2), news they have learned from Rahab.

The crossing of the Jordan River, the river marking the boundary of the Promised Land, is an occasion of wonders comparable to the crossing of the Red Sea (4:23; cf. 3:7; 4:14). The great significance of these wonders is indicated in 4:24. They are to remain a testimony for all peoples for all time that the hand of the Lord is powerful. The prominence of the ark of the covenant (3:3 note) relates God’s power to His promises that are at the heart of the covenant. Chapter 3 gives the events in order; ch. 4 returns to and elaborates on several points, especially the memorial of stones at Gilgal.

In light of Joshua’s instructions in 1:11, it is probable that 3:1 looks back in time, introducing events that took place at the same time as the actions of the spies in ch. 2. We are not told that the spies returned to Shittim before the Israelites left there.

verse_quote: the ark of the covenant of the
note:
LORD **your God.** See Ex. 25:10–22; Deut. 10:5. The ark plays a prominent role in chs. 3; 4; 6; and 8. As the footstool to the heavenly throne (1 Chron. 28:2), it signifies not only the presence of the Lord (Num. 10:33–36) but specifically His covenant, which means His commitment to His promises as well as the consequent obligations of Israel. See notes on 1:5; 24:25.

**the Levitical priests.** See Deut. 10:8.

verse_quote: a distance between you and it.
note: The purpose of the separation may be to ensure that the ark will be visible to the maximum number of people. See 4:11.

“Consecrate” means “to make holy” (5:15 note), and probably refers to physical actions, such as washing, that symbolize the holiness of the people. There was a similar requirement when God came down to the people at Mount Sinai (Ex. 19:10, 14, 15).

**wonders.** The same word is used of the miraculous events in Egypt (Ex. 3:20; Judg. 6:13; Ps. 78:11; Mic. 7:15) and the conquest of Canaan (Ex. 34:10; 1 Chr. 16:9–24; cf. Jer. 21:2).

verse_quote: I will begin to exalt you.
note:
The Lord validates Joshua’s leadership by repeating the wonders He did at the Red Sea through Moses (Ex. 14–15). The God of Joshua is the God of Moses. See note on 4:14.

**that they may know.** God’s acts bring about knowledge (Ex. 8:10; Deut. 4:35; 2 Kin. 19:19; Is. 45:6), and such knowledge is never merely intellectual. It does not bypass the intellect, however, as it is attainable by hearing the news of God’s acts and by seeing them (2:9, 10; 4:24). Here the object of knowledge is the presence of God with Joshua (1:5 note; cf. Ex. 14:31), which the people will experience through the faithfulness of God to His promises. See notes on v. 10; 4:24.

verse_quote: listen to the words of the
note: LORD **.** A fundamental duty of the people of God. See 1:8; 24:2.

The reference is probably to the entire miracle of the crossing, but attention is focused on the role of the ark (v. 11).

**know.** That is, “know by experience” (cf. v. 7). Israel will know the presence of God with them to bring His promise to certain fulfillment. Remarkably, Rahab has already attained this knowledge (2:9).

**the living God.** Israel’s God is opposed to and contrasted with lifeless idols (Deut. 32:21).

**Canaanites ... Jebusites.** One of several ways of listing the inhabitants of Canaan (Gen. 15:18–21; Deut. 7:1). See note on 2:10.

verse_quote: the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth.
note: Lit. “the ark of the covenant, the Lord of all the earth.” Not only the symbol of the covenant but the Lord Himself will go ahead of His people. The reminder that He is Lord of all the earth suggests that the events to follow have a purpose that reaches beyond Israel (4:24; cf. 2:11; Gen. 12:3; Ex. 19:5, 6).
Anticipates the main subject of ch. 4; see 4:2.
The language has similarities to Ex. 15:8 and Ps. 78:13, which describe the crossing of the Red Sea (4:23). The God of the exodus is the God who will settle the Israelites in Canaan.
This verse picks up the action from v. 6.
This vital piece of information takes the reader by surprise. The crossing will be even more remarkable than was indicated in v. 13.
A site on the eastern bank of the Jordan River approximately sixteen miles (26 km) north of Jericho.
As instrumental in the miracle, the ark conveys the powerful message of God’s royal presence and his faithfulness to His covenant promises.
All Israel is to be represented (1:12–15).

This testimony for future generations of God’s faithfulness is the first of several in Joshua (7:26; 8:29). See note on v. 9.

**What do those stones mean.** Ex. 12:26, 27; Deut. 6:20–25.

As the ark is prominent in ch. 3, so is it central to the retelling of the story to future generations. See notes on 3:3, 17.

**memorial.** The purpose of the “sign” (v. 6) and telling about it is for future generations to remember God’s faithfulness to His promises. On the importance of Israel’s remembering, see Deut. 8:1–20; 1 Cor. 11:25; 2 Tim. 2:8.

That is, the day of the narrator. This expression occurs frequently in Joshua (5:9; 6:25; 7:26; 8:28, 29; 9:27; 10:27; 13:13; 14:14; 15:63; 16:10), evidencing the truth and relevance of the narrative.
Some scholars suggest that the word translated “thousand” means a military unit of unspecified size, a “contingent.”

LORD **exalted Joshua ... and they stood in awe of him.** Joshua’s exaltation is in fulfillment of 3:7 (cf. Ex. 14:31). God’s powerful faithfulness to His promises has the effect of exalting the one whose leadership is based on those promises.
The conclusion of the miracle is described, with the focus still on the ark.
Also called the “ark of the covenant” (Ex. 25:16, 21, 22; 31:18; 32:15; 40:20). The Ten Commandments were deposited in the ark as a testimony to the agreement God made with Israel.

verse_quote: the tenth day of the first month.
note: The day the Passover lamb is chosen (Ex. 12:3), underlining the connection between the crossing and the exodus. See v. 23 and 5:10.

The pronoun “you” identifies the later generations with the earlier great acts of God, as Moses did in Deut. 4:9–24; 5:2–5, and as Joshua will do in Josh. 24:5–10 (24:7 note).

**4:24 all the peoples of the earth.** The wonders of chs. 3 and 4 will have effects far beyond both the immediate generation and the Israelite people (2:10; 5:1; cf. Gen. 12:3). The works of God powerfully affect not only those who see them but also those who hear about them (Ex. 10:2; John 20:30, 31). See notes 2:9, 10.

**know.** The knowledge of God and His purposes has been the objective of these wonders (3:7, 10 notes), a goal now shown to apply to all peoples. Such knowledge does not necessarily imply salvation (Ex. 14:18).

**fear the** LORD **.** A common OT expression for true faith (Ps. 128:1). See 24:14 note.

A significant moment (v. 9), with the wilderness behind them and the new life in the Land of Promise before them (vv. 11, 12), is marked by two symbolic actions: circumcision (vv. 2–8) and the Passover (v. 10). Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Gen. 17:9–14 notes) and was required for participation in the Passover (Ex. 12:48). Circumcision marked the people of the promise; the Passover celebrated their redemption from Egypt. Both the promise to Abraham and the redemption from Egypt looked forward to this day of crossing and conquest (Gen. 17:8; Ex. 3:8).

**5:1 As soon as all the kings ... heard.** See 4:24; note on 2:9.

**Amorites.** See note on 2:10.

**Canaanites.** Probably refers to those who lived in the lower regions of the land (Num. 13:29; 14:25; Deut. 1:7).
See v. 5.

This circumcision is necessary because the generation that came out of Egypt had fallen under God’s judgment. In His grace God is raising up a new generation for Himself (v. 7). Physical circumcision has its spiritual counterpart in circumcised hearts (Deut. 10:16; 30:6 and notes).

LORD **.** The simplest description of the behavior that brought judgment. The reference is to Num. 14 (Deut. 1:32, 43).

**the** LORD **swore.** The promise of God can be negative.
These people are, in effect, a “new Israel.”

verse_quote: Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt.
note:
These words indicate the great significance of this moment. The redemption from Egypt is complete only with the entry into the Promised Land. See the promise of the exodus and its goal in Ex. 3:8. Had that goal not been reached, the reproach or scorn of Egypt would have remained (Deut. 9:28).

**to this day.** See note on 4:9.
Another indication that a new era has begun, and the first major section of the book is concluded; see Introduction: Outline. On manna and its significance, see Ex. 16; Deut. 8:3.

The second major section of the book describes how the Israelites subdue Canaan. It is commonly thought that the Israelite invasion was accompanied by widespread violence and destruction. Yet, the book of Joshua records only three cities being razed by the Israelites—Jericho (6:24), Ai (8:28), and Hazor (11:11)—and in each instance, the Israelites give their enemies an opportunity to avoid death by abandoning their territory or, as with Rahab, seeking refuge in Israel’s God. While every opportunity is given for people to flee from the Israelites, those who resist forfeit their lives. As Gen. 15:16 reveals, the Israelites are to take possession of the land only when the sin of the Amorites has reached its full measure. In a similar fashion, Lev. 18:25 states that the expulsion of Canaan’s descendants is due to their defiling of the land. Leviticus uses the image of the land vomiting out its inhabitants, a motif that associates possession of the land with righteous behavior and loss of land with immoral behavior. In light of this, Israel’s seizure of Canaan is a vivid reminder of the reality of divine judgment upon those who by their unrighteous actions lose their land. These accounts of destruction, no less than anything else in the book, prefigure God’s final judgment on those who reject His grace (Matt. 25:46; Heb. 9:27; 10:26–31).

**5:13–15** The account of the conquest begins with the appearance of “the commander of the army of the LORD,” which shows that God, not Joshua, controls the ensuing action. Joshua is the servant of the same God who appeared to Moses in the burning bush (Ex. 3:5).

The commander of the Lord’s army encourages Joshua, but He is not under Joshua’s command. God is bound neither to destroy all Canaanites nor to deliver all Israelites, as is powerfully illustrated in the subsequent chapters in the experiences of Rahab (6:25) and Achan (ch. 7). See notes on 6:17, 18.

**commander of the army of the** LORD **.** Some scholars believe that the commander is an appearance of the preincarnate Son of God. As v. 15 reveals, the ground is made holy by God’s presence. The divine warrior and His army are prepared for war, reassuring Joshua of victory.

This command is like that of Ex. 3:5, establishing a continuity between what began with Moses and what follows under Joshua. Joshua is the successor to Moses. Holiness is fundamentally a quality of God. People (3:5 note) or things are described as holy when they belong to God in some special way.

Its name means “moon,” implying that the city is a center for astral worship in Joshua’s time.

**6:1–27** The essential elements for a theological understanding of the Israelite conquest of Canaan are indicated in this account of Jericho, the first city to be destroyed. The destruction of the Canaanites, no less than the crossing of the Jordan, is the powerful work of the sovereign God (note the role of the ark of the covenant in chs. 3, 4, and 6; see notes on 3:3, 11, 14, 17; 4:16). The fearful judgment of God working to bring about the promised deliverance of His people is an important biblical theme (e.g., Ex. 14:13–14; Rev. 19:1–2). Furthermore, that the grace of God is not restricted to Israel (Gen. 12:3) is evidenced by the experience of Rahab and her household (v. 25). Here we observe the principle that faith in God saves despite physical descent. God is not simply anti-Canaanite (see note 5:14). Moreover, the people of Jericho are given six days in which to escape from the city.

LORD **.** Probably refers to the “commander of the army of the LORD” (5:13–15), although these verses may be part of a separate episode introducing the whole of the conquest of Jericho.

**See, I have given.** A striking paradox, since all that has been seen is Jericho’s shut gates (v. 1). The promise of God creates possibilities not inherent in the present situation. The contrast between present circumstances and God’s promises is found often in the Bible (Gen. 15:2–5; Is. 65:17; Rom. 8:18).

Suggests a parallel to the work of creation. Just as the work of creation reached its goal in the seventh day (Gen. 2:1–3), so the work of redemption from Egypt reaches its goal with possession of the Promised Land. Sabbath rest is related to both creation and redemption (Ex. 20:8–11; Deut. 5:12–15; Josh. 1:13 note). In Heb. 3:7–4:11 “rest” refers to the ultimate goal of God’s people.
The collapse of the wall will allow access from every direction.

See note 3:3. The procession, with the ark at its center, applies the covenant promises of God symbolically to Jericho. For Jericho, the covenant promises will mean judgment as the city stands in opposition to God.
LORD **.** As in 3:11 (note), the presence of the ark is identified with the presence of the Lord Himself. See note on 1:5.

The whole procession can be summed up with reference only to the ark.

**in the camp.** At Gilgal (5:10).

The description of the seventh day is expanded with a report of Joshua’s speech. In accordance with the narrative style noted elsewhere (1:11; 2:6 and notes), the words of vv. 17–19 may have been spoken earlier but are recorded here for dramatic effect.

Holy war involves the awful reality of God’s judgment on Jericho, as also on the whole of Canaan (11:11–12, 14, 20; Lev. 27:28–29; Deut. 13:16; 20:10–18). All that is captured in battle is to be given over to God, which involves the death of everyone—men, women, and children (e.g., Deut. 2:34; 3:6). While people and property are devoted to destruction frequently in Joshua (2:10; 6:17, 18, 21; 7:1, 11–15; 8:26; 10:1, 28, 35–40; 11:11–12, 20–21; 19:38; 22:20), earlier passages speak of the Israelites “dispossessing” or “expelling” the nations of Canaan. It is therefore noteworthy that the concept of total destruction in war was first introduced in the context of the Israelites being attacked by the Canaanite king of Arad (Num. 21:1–3). Later, Deut. 2:34 and 3:6 apply the same concept to Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, both of whom deliberately attack the Israelites. A survey of the book of Joshua also suggests that the concept of total destruction is applied only to those who are actively hostile toward the Israelites. Since such hostility is actually directed against God, all those involved forfeit their right to life.

**Only Rahab ... and all who are with her.** Judgment on Canaan does not exclude grace. The mercy she sought in 2:12 will be extended to her.
The same Hebrew term found in v. 17 occurs three times here, warning Israel not to fall into the same judgment as the Canaanites. Chapter 7 shows the need for this warning.
See note on 5:15.
The fall of Jericho is briefly described. Further details may be deduced from v. 24; 8:2; 10:1; 24:11., 21
This phrase can describe a temporary state of affairs (v. 25) due to ceremonial uncleanness (e.g., Lev. 13:46).
LORD **.** See note on 9:23.

Rahab is included in the people of God. See Matt. 1:5; Heb. 11:31; James 2:25.

**to this day.** See note on 4:9.

verse_quote: Cursed ... who rises up and rebuilds.
note: Jericho is to remain under God’s curse, presumably as a sign of God’s judgment, which had fallen on the Canaanites and could fall on Israel. See 1 Kin. 16:34.
LORD **was with Joshua.** See note on 4:14.

If the story of Rahab, the Canaanite who found mercy, reveals God’s grace in the midst of judgment (6:25), Achan’s story is a reminder of God’s holiness—on which no one may presume (24:19; Num. 17:11–13; Heb. 10:30, 31). Unbelief destroys, regardless of physical descent. Chapter 7 recounts the first instance of disobedience in the Promised Land, an ominous event in light of the history that follows (2 Kin. 17:7–20) and an occasion reminiscent of Gen. 3 (v. 21 note). The incident and its lesson for Israel are recalled in 22:18–20.

**7:1 the people of Israel.** Although the offense was committed by one man, all Israel is involved and affected (see v. 11; 22:18). The facts stated in v. 1 only gradually became known to the Israelites.

**devoted things.** See 6:18; note on 6:17.

**the anger of the** LORD **.** The anger of God is His personal, righteous hostility to evil. Unlike ancient pagan conceptions of divine wrath, God’s anger is never arbitrary or capricious. It is as much a part of the NT message as it is of the OT (Matt. 3:7; John 3:36; Rom. 1:18; Col. 3:6; 1 Thess. 1:10; Heb. 10:26–31; Rev. 6:16).

In contrast to the stories of the spies (ch. 2) and the conquest of Jericho (ch. 6), Israel is now under God’s anger, and the outcome will be different.

**7:2 from Jericho to Ai.** The movement is westward and up into the central hill country. The Israelites are attempting to secure the center of Canaan before proceeding to conquer the southern and northern regions.

**Beth-aven.** The name means “house of nothingness” or “house of wickedness,” and is on occasion used disparagingly of Bethel (as in Hos. 4:15; 10:5).

verse_quote: Do not have all the people go up.
note: Cf. the report of the spies in 2:24.

The number of casualties is not great. The fear and dismay of the people are due more to the Lord’s anger than to the human scale of the defeat.

This summary of the conquest under Joshua approximates the account so far given but with additions, indicating the incomplete and representative nature of the preceding account. Although Joshua is never designated a king, his ability to lead the Israelites to victory against the kings of Canaan is underlined by the list of defeated kings.

The third major section of the book details the division of the land among the tribes. The significance of these chapters is made explicit in 21:43–45. The lists of boundaries and towns represent the objective content of God’s promises. However, many of the places are no longer known, and their allotment here does not in all cases mean that the designated tribe actually occupies them at this point in Israel’s history (23:13). Nevertheless, these allotments are an elaborate testimony to the faithfulness of the Lord. Note also the important contrast drawn between some of the tribes. Whereas Judah, Ephraim, and half of Manasseh have actively taken possession of territory in Joshua’s lifetime, the tribes of Benjamin, Simeon, Zeb­ulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan have yet to settle in their allocated regions. The prominence given to Judah, in particular, anticipates how that tribe will provide leadership for the whole nation of Israel through the Davidic dynasty. Though the tribe of Ephraim enjoys the privilege of being the leading tribe in the time of Joshua, the book of Judges will chronicle the tribe’s fall from divine favor, something already signaled by its reluctance to overthrow the Canaanites in the Valley of Jezreel and in Beth Shan (17:16–18).

While the book of Joshua testifies to Israel’s experience of the Lord’s faithfulness, the land of Canaan will only be fully settled after the death of Joshua.

At the end of his life Joshua leads Israel in a reaffirmation of the covenant, much as Moses did before he died (Deut. 32:46). As with Deuteronomy, there may be an analogy between this covenant renewal and the kind of treaties that were typically used to formalize relations between powerful sovereign nations and weaker client states in the ancient Near East (see Deuteronomy: Introduction). Called “suzerainty treaties,” they commonly included elements such as those found in Josh. 24: a historical prologue reviewing the care given by the powerful party to the client (vv. 2–13); a prohibition of any outside alliance (vv. 14, 23); and provision for a written document (vv. 25, 26). There are also significant differences between such ancient treaties and Josh. 24.
